The ASX briefly drops by 1%, coincides with bonds selloff
The ASX 200 opened sharply lower at 0.77% after a rebound in oil prices and government borrowing costs. It briefly dropped by 1.16% on Thursday morning before bouncing back a little.
The dip coincided with bond yields reaching new highs on Wall St, prompting a sell off.
David Clewell, co-portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price, said that a perfect storm had led to a selloff of US 10-year Treasury bonds.

"The 5% level on the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield has been an important psychological threshold for investors, effectively marking the upper end of the range since the post COVID period," the analyst said.
"Once a key technical level like this is breached, systematic and quantitative positioning can amplify the move and lead to further selling."
The stronger than expected economic data that came out of the US overnight, coupled with these high bond yields, provided a "catalyst" for an "unusually sharp" selloff.
New Zealand house prices also slump
We reported earlier that Australian house prices have fallen for the sixth straight month and experts predict further drops of up to 15 per cent in the near future.

Our little cousin over the water also isn't immune to housing woes, with New Zealand home prices also slipping every month for the past half year according to the latest results from property data firm Cotality.
New Zealand’s home prices dropped to their lowest point in nearly six years in September.
The Home Value Index declined 0.3 per cent from August, to their lowest points since January 2021.
Cotality NZ chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said the numbers were far from the 2021 peak in New Zealand but said that overall property values remained "resilient".

Why is oil price still high when crude exports are near pre-war levels?
Can you explain why oil is rising when ive recently read that oil movement is back to ~98% pre-war levels. - Vas
Can you explain why oil is rising when ive recently read that oil movement is back to ~98% pre-war levels.
- Vas
Hey Vas, good question.
There are indeed reports that crude oil exports are nearly at pre-war levels.
Crude oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz hit a seven-day average of 13.5 million barrels a day as of Monday, according to data from tanker tracker group Kpler.
Goldman Sachs put that figure higher, estimating that exports reached 19 million barrels a day over the past week through Monday.

JP Morgan said it was around 17.5 million barrels a day, which is sitting at 95 per cent of pre-war levels. However, the recovery is "uneven" and the refinery supply remains "constrained", according to Natasha Kaneva, head of global commodities at JP Morgan.
Uncertainty remains about how long it will keep flowing out of the Persian Gulf, especially as US-Iran talks stall.
Due to infrastructure damage, including at refineries, JP Morgan estimates that exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel are only at about half their 2025 levels, at 58 per cent.
"The biggest source of pain is the diesel market,” Francisco Blanch, head of global commodities at Bank of America, told CNBC on Wednesday.
And there are fears of more shipping disruption on the horizon.
Trump says Powell should be 'forced' to resign from Federal Reserve
Over in the US, President Donald Trump is calling for former Federal Reserve chief Jerome Powell's resignation.

The fresh calls come following the Federal Reserve's Inspector General saying it found no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to cost overruns in a US central bank renovation project.

The Fed watchdog's report highlighted extensive problems with project oversight that contributed to a roughly US$1 billion cost overrun for the renovation of the central bank's two historic buildings on the National Mall in Washington.

Trump has latched onto the cost overrun on the project, which now has a price tag of about US$2.4 billion, in his effort to engineer Powell's ouster and gain influence over the direction of monetary policy. Trump is also trying to sack Fed Governor Lisa Cook over alleged wrongdoing in an unrelated matter.
Powell declined to comment on the report, the latest chapter in an ongoing feud with Trump that goes back to 2018, when the president first criticised the Fed chief for not cutting interest rates.

"At a minimum, 'Too Late' Powell should be forced to resign from the Board. He can’t manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn’t be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on “TRUMP!”)," the president wrote on Truth Social.
"If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable."
Reporting with Reuters
EV monthly sales hits all-time high as oil crisis continues
August was an all-time high for electric vehicle sales across Australia, in a sign of a lack of confidence in the oil crisis abating any time soon.
The latest vehicle sales data showed the share of electric vehicle sales hit 24.9 per cent in August, the highest ever.
Hybrids came in at 9.7 per cent, nearly reaching the highs of sales figures in June at 11. 5 per cent.
In a note this morning, Commonwealth Bank's sustainable and energy economist John Oh said "the continued strong EV sales suggest fuel price hikes were the initial catalyst for the lift in EV demand".
He noted that tax benefits and favourable novated leases were also driving the trend.
Electric vehicle sales from Chinese brands surged by 266 per cent for the year to August.
This lifted Chinese brands' share of the Australian EV market to 59 per cent, way up from this time last year where it was sitting at 38 per cent.
It comes as petrol and diesel prices rose as much as 48 and 77 per cent, respectively, above pre-war levels across March and April.
A report from the Electric Vehicle Council released yesterday revealed that an electric car is being sold every 100 seconds in Australia.
ICYMI: October 9 is D-day for mortgage holders as big four pass on rate rise
In case you missed it last night, all four of the big four banks have passed on Tuesday's rate rises to mortgage borrowers.

Macquarie Bank was the first to move on Tuesday, confirming it was passing on the 25-point rise in full to customers moments after the Reserve Bank announced the hike, bringing the cash rate to 4.60%.
The Commonwealth Bank was the first of the big four to increase interest rates, effective from October 9.
Westpac, NAB and ANZ were quick to follow suit passing on the hikes to borrowers.
Tuesday's rate rise brings levels to the highest they've been in 15 years.
September was brutal for the bonds market, worst month in years
Global bonds ended September with the worst month they've had in years, experts have warned.
Two-year borrowing costs in France, Germany, the UK and Australia recorded their biggest monthly jumps since March when the Iran war started.
Over in Japan, government bond yields are pinned near multi-decade highs.
Meanwhile, 10-year US Treasury bonds posted their biggest monthly yield increase since 2022 and biggest jump in a quarter since 2009.
France's 10-year yields suffered their biggest monthly rise in almost four years.
"There's a realisation that the whole energy story and inflation story will not go away in the very short term," said Societe Generale's head of corporate research for FX and rates Kenneth Broux.
"Bond markets are adjusting to that."
"Bond markets are adjusting to that."

My colleague David Taylor reported over the weekend that bonds are generally considered an economic canary in the coal mine. So when bonds aren't going well it's a sign of broader financial market stress.
With Reuters
Property prices drop for sixth month straight
Cotality's Home Value Index fell 1.1% in September taking cumulative declines to 5.2% below March's peak.
Brisbane saw the sharpest monthly drop among capitals (-1.5%), while Sydney saw a 1.4% fall and Melbourne was down 0.7%.
Darwin (+0.4%) was the only housing market to avoid a fall.

More than 1,000 large companies paid no tax
Data from the Australian Tax Office shows almost 30 per cent of large companies paid no tax in 2024–25.
The ATO's 12th corporate tax transparency report found there were 1,149 entities that did not pay tax during that period.
The tax office is watching companies that use offshore financing and marketing hubs, as well as AI businesses.

US inflation figures released overnight less than expected
Inflation figures released overnight from the US were less than expected, but still rose, sparking fears of another rate hike.

Headline inflation rose by 0.3 per cent for the month, bringing the rate to 3.4 per cent for the year to August. The core Personal Consumption Expenditure rose by 0.2 per cent for the month, bringing the annual rate to 3 per cent.
The figures were better than expected, with initial estimates putting headline inflation at the 3.7 per cent mark.
The US central bank hiked interest rates in September, for the first time in three years, amid inflation fears.
Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, said inflation was "still miles above target".
“We said after September’s hike it wouldn’t be the last one this year, and we’re sticking with that call," he said.
